title: Words are coloured for their role and their background
when: Whenever a shot puts words on screen: titles, numbers, keywords, posters, labels.
summary: A word's colour decides whether it is read first, read at all, or felt as part of the picture. Pale words on a bright place vanish; one strong warm colour on the key word makes the eye land there. The same idea keeps the same colour across the video, so colour starts to mean something.
do: Give the key word, number or verdict the accent or a strong warm colour (gold, yellow, orange, red).
Keep supporting words in the ink colour, and two or three word colours per shot at most.
Check what lies behind the word: light colours over dark or busy places, dark colours over light ones.
Give a big poster word behind people a rich colour taken from the scene, so it belongs to the picture.
avoid: a pale or white word over a sky, a cloud or a light map
a new colour for the same idea in a later scene
every word in the accent colour
source: Owner review 2026-10-19 (a pale poster word); video-use manim-video references visual-design.md 'colour = meaning' (MIT, pinned 43cfc56); restated in our own words.

title: The picture arrives a moment before the words name it
when: When timing what appears on screen against the narration.
summary: When the viewer sees a thing just before hearing its name, the picture primes the word and both land together. When they hear it first, they search the screen for something that is not there yet and lose the next sentence.
do: Start a reveal so its landing frame falls on the spoken payoff word (start it the reveal's length earlier).
Let a drawing or a title lead its word by a few frames, never trail it.
avoid: a number appearing after the narrator has already moved on
reveals timed to the start of the sentence instead of the word that names them
source: video-use SKILL.md 'animation payoff timing' and manim-video animation-design-thinking.md 'see then hear' (MIT, pinned 43cfc56), restated.

title: One new idea at a time, with room to read it
when: When a shot introduces a concept, a number, a label or a diagram.
summary: The eye tracks one or two new things at once. A shot that reveals several independent things together means none of them registers, and the viewer is still reading when the next shot cuts in.
do: Reveal one thing, pause, then the next; build a diagram part by part on its words.
Give a new idea time to be read: a short label about a second, a key insight several seconds and a held beat after it.
Vary the tempo: slow builds for the core idea, quick runs for lists, a held pause before the big reveal.
Leave real empty space in the frame (about a sixth) so the new thing has somewhere to land.
avoid: two unrelated things arriving together
the same duration for every reveal
more than five or six things on screen at once
source: video-use manim-video references animation-design-thinking.md and visual-design.md (MIT, pinned 43cfc56), restated.

title: Show the destination dimmed, then light it part by part
when: When a whole (a sentence, a chart, a system, a list) is explained one part at a time.
summary: Showing the whole dimmed first tells the viewer where the explanation is going; lighting one part at a time keeps attention on the part being spoken while the rest stays as context.
steps: Show the whole quietly (dim or small).
Light the first part as it is named; dim it a little when the next part is named.
End with the whole lit, so the last frame is the summary.
do: Use the order the viewer needs to understand, not the order the parts sit in.
For a big system: overview, zoom into one part, back out, zoom into the next.
avoid: building a long line left to right with no hint of where it ends
source: video-use manim-video references animation-design-thinking.md 'dim and reveal', 'zoom and return' (MIT, pinned 43cfc56), restated.

title: Zooms grow the area evenly
when: Whenever the camera zooms, or a thing grows from small to full size.
summary: A scale that grows linearly seems to rush at first and crawl at the end, because the eye reads area. Interpolating the area (scale squared) and taking its square root makes a zoom feel steady.

numbers.scale(q): sqrt(a^2 + (b^2 - a^2) * q) for q from 0 to 1

do: Use the area rule for camera zooms, focus zooms and grow entrances; ease the timing on top of it.
avoid: linear scale tweens for big zooms
source: Remotion interpolate() output 'perceptual-scale' (Remotion License, pinned a65368a; idea only, no code copied).

title: Expo-out landings, critically damped pushes, never linear
when: When choosing how anything moves into place.
summary: Linear motion looks robotic. A fast start with a long settle (a curve like cubic-bezier 0.16, 1, 0.3, 1) reads as confident; a spring with heavy damping gives a push without bounce. Bounce is a spice for one payoff, not a default.
do: Land things with a fast-start, long-settle curve.
Use a heavily damped spring for pushes and camera reframes.
Keep overshoot for the single biggest payoff of a video.
avoid: linear tweens
a springy bounce on everything
source: Remotion skills remotion-markup timing.md (pinned 1441a11) and video-use SKILL.md easing (MIT), restated.

title: Hand-made looks may animate on twos
when: When a video's look is hand-made: whiteboard, doodle, storybook, pencil, paper cut-outs.
summary: Hand-drawn animation traditionally holds each drawing for two or three frames. Stepped motion makes a hand-made look feel crafted instead of computer-smooth; it is a style choice, not a rule.
do: Consider drawing.cadence 'twos' for doodle, storybook and whiteboard styles; 'threes' for a stop-motion feel.
Keep motion blur off when animating on twos.
avoid: stepped motion on footage or on fast camera moves meant to feel smooth
source: Remotion skills timing.md 'posterization' (pinned 1441a11), restated; classic 2D animation practice.

title: Fast moves get a camera's motion blur
when: When something crosses the frame quickly: a whip in, a slide, a slam, a crash zoom.
summary: Real cameras blur fast motion over the shutter's open time (a 180-degree shutter is half a frame). Without it, fast designed motion strobes. Hand-made looks show speed with smears and lines instead, so blur is for designed and filmic shots.
do: Blur designed motion graphics on their fast moves only; keep still frames sharp.
Use enough samples that the copies merge into a smear.
avoid: blurring every frame
photographic blur on thin-outlined cartoon art
source: Remotion motion-blur CameraMotionBlur (Remotion License, pinned a65368a; idea only), restated.

title: An overlay can dress a cut without shortening the film
when: When a hard cut needs energy or warmth but a crossfade would blur the story.
summary: A transition overlaps two shots and shortens the timeline; an overlay (a light leak, a flash, a burn) plays on top of a hard cut and keeps every frame. Overlays keep the cut's precision and still give the moment character.
do: Use a light leak or flash over a hard cut for a warm or energetic change.
Count a transition's overlap when you time the narration to the picture.
avoid: crossfades on every scene change
an overlay and a transition on the same cut
source: Remotion skills transitions.md and light-leaks.md (pinned 1441a11), restated.

title: Check your own render at every cut before anyone sees it
when: After a render, before the owner reviews it.
summary: Most visible faults sit at boundaries: a flash, a jump, an overlay hiding a caption, an audio pop. Looking at a strip of frames and the waveform around each cut catches them faster than watching the whole video.
checks: Each cut: no flash, no unplanned jump, no waveform spike.
Captions are never hidden by an overlay (captions are always the top layer).
First two seconds, last two seconds and a few middle points: the grade and the captions hold.
Measure loudness and true peak; report numbers, never 'it sounds good'.
At most three fix-and-check passes, then list what is left for the owner.
source: video-use SKILL.md 'self-eval' and hard rules (MIT, pinned 43cfc56), restated.

title: Match the shots first, then grade by looking
when: When footage from different sources is cut together, or a grade is chosen.
summary: Stock from many cameras differs in exposure and contrast; a creative grade on top of mismatched clips makes the mismatch worse. Gently level each clip first, then apply one grade, and judge it on a real frame: change one thing, look again. Skin tones are the test.
steps: Level each clip a little (bounded, colour balance kept).
Apply one grade to every clip.
Look at a frame with a face; adjust one thing at a time.
do: Think in lift (shadows), gamma (mids) and gain (highlights), then saturation.
avoid: a strong look without checking skin
a different grade per clip without a story reason
source: video-use SKILL.md 'color grade' and helpers/grade.py auto-grade (MIT, pinned 43cfc56), restated.

title: Captions are chunked by speech and style
when: When narration is cut into on-screen captions.
summary: Captions read best when their breaks follow the voice: punctuation and pauses end a caption, a flash under about a third of a second is unreadable, and the style decides the size of a chunk (two or three words for fast social cuts, four to seven for documentary).
do: Break on punctuation and pauses; grow a chunk rather than flash a tiny one.
Use word-level timings, never phrase-level ones.
Pick the look to suit the video: clean, bold capitals, boxed, cinematic, glow, comic or pop.
avoid: captions behind overlays
a caption that cuts a word in half
source: video-use SKILL.md subtitles (MIT), caption-ai themes and chunk merge (MIT, pinned 5779ef6), Remotion captions paging (idea), restated.

title: Fewer sound effects, each hitting its frame
when: When sound effects are placed under picture events.
summary: Generated videos sound cheap when every transition has a whoosh. A few effects tied to visible events read as designed. Most effects build before their hit, so the file must start early by that build or the hit lands late.
do: Tie every effect to something visible: a cut, a landing, a stamp.
Start the file its attack earlier so the hit lands on the contact frame.
Duck music under speech and let it end before a stinger.
avoid: an effect on every transition
effects louder than the voice
source: video-use SKILL.md 'music and sound effects' (MIT, pinned 43cfc56), restated.

title: Narration pace stays in the comfortable band
when: When a narration is directed or reviewed.
summary: Comfortable narration runs about 140-160 words a minute; above about 170 it sounds rushed and below about 110 it drags. Measuring words per minute is more reliable than re-generating takes and hoping.
do: Slow the delivery for dense or emotional passages; speed up lists only a little.
avoid: a whole narration above 170 words a minute
source: claude-code-video-toolkit tools/pacing.py (MIT, pinned 959e0fc), restated.

title: Watch a video coarse first, then dense where it matters
when: When a reference or competitor video is analysed.
summary: Every frame of a ten-minute video is thousands of images, so looking at all of them wastes the budget and buries the signal. A coarse pass (about fifty frames plus every scene change) finds the structure, and dense windows answer the questions that matter (the hook, a reveal, a transition).
steps: Overview: evenly spaced frames plus scene-change frames across the whole video.
Read the platform's own captions when they exist; never generate a transcript of someone else's video.
Dense passes (a few frames a second) only around the hook, payoffs and anything uncertain.
Split long videos into chapters or ten-minute windows and keep one running timeline.
avoid: signing in, using cookies or getting around access controls
frame-by-frame scans of the whole video
source: watch-video SKILL.md and references/analysis-protocol.md (MIT, pinned 9492ba3), restated.

title: Every finding says whether it was seen, said or inferred
when: When a video analysis or review reports what a video does.
summary: A transcript claim is not visual proof, and a conclusion is not an observation. Labelling each finding keeps analyses honest and shows where evidence is missing.
do: Label each finding observed (in a frame), spoken (in captions) or inferred (reasoned from both).
Mark support: supported, conflicted or not found; give a confidence and its reason.
Give every finding a bounded timestamp and the frame or caption it rests on.
avoid: describing a spoken claim as something the video shows
guessing identity or intent without evidence
source: watch-video references/analysis-protocol.md evidence model (MIT, pinned 9492ba3), restated.

title: A skill earns its place by beating no-skill on real tasks
when: When a skill is written, changed or doubted.
summary: A skill can feel helpful and still change nothing. Running the same task with and without it, and letting a judge compare the outputs without knowing which is which, shows whether it helps; reading why the winner won shows what to keep.
steps: Pick two or three real tasks the skill should improve.
Run each with the skill and without it (or with the previous version).
Compare blind; write down why the better one is better.
Keep what helped, cut what did nothing, explain the why in the skill, test again.
avoid: rules in capitals with no reason
fixing one example so hard that the skill stops generalising
keeping lines that never change an output
source: anthropics/skills skill-creator SKILL.md (Apache-2.0, pinned dbd4588), restated.

title: Write skills that explain why
when: When a new skill is drafted or an old one rewritten.
summary: A capable model follows reasons better than commands: a rule with its reason generalises to cases the rule never named, while a bare command in capitals is followed narrowly or ignored. Lean skills that say when they apply and why work best.
do: Say when the skill applies.
Give the reason behind each rule.
Keep the skill short; move long references out.
avoid: rules shouted in capitals with no reason
a skill longer than the brief it will be read in
source: anthropics/skills skill-creator SKILL.md 'writing style' (Apache-2.0, pinned dbd4588), restated.

title: Hand-made looks use real media textures
when: When a style is pencil, crayon, storybook, painted or watercolour.
summary: A clean vector line reads as computer-made. Real media have tooth and pressure: a pencil line is darker where the hand presses and broken where the paper's grain lies; a watercolour wash is uneven and darker at its rim. These textures are what make a hand-made look believable.
do: Let places be washed in; keep characters solid so they stay readable.
Use graphite for pencil sketches, crayon tooth for doodles, coloured pencil for storybooks.
avoid: transparent watercolour on characters
the same texture on every look
source: p5.brush (MIT, Alejandro Campos Uribe, pinned 43ac6d5) brushes, pressure and watercolour fill; Tyler Hobbs' watercolour method; restated.

title: Use fonts this PC really has
when: When a style or a design names a font.
summary: A font that is not installed is replaced silently by another face, so a design ships in the wrong letters with no error. Check the font exists, or name a look-alike that does.
do: Pick fonts the program reports as installed.
When a font is missing, accept the named look-alike or install the font.
avoid: web fonts in a design that renders offline
source: video-use SKILL.md 'fonts fail silently' (MIT, pinned 43cfc56), restated.
